f′(x)=u′(x)⋅v(x)−u(x)v′(x)[v(x)]2=(1)⋅(2x2−11x+5)−(x+1)⋅(4x−11)(2x2−11x+5)2=2x2−11x+5−(4x2−11x+4x−11)(2x2−11x+5)2=2x2−11x+5−4x2+11x−4x+11(2x2−11x+5)2=−2x2−4x+16(2x2−11x+5)2=−2(x2+2x−8)(2x2−11x+5)2.

The slope of the tangent line to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at $x=1$ is

q-129624.worked_solution:
The slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(1).$ In part 1, we found

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{-2({x}^{2}+2x-8)}{(2{x}^{2}-11x+5)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=1,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{-2({1}^{2}+2\cdot 1-8)}{(2\cdot {1}^{2}-11\cdot 1+5)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{16} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line to the curve at $x=1$ is $\frac{5}{8}.$

q-129625.worked_solution:
In part 2 we found that ${f}^{′}(1)=\frac{5}{8}.$ Also,

$$
f(1)=\frac{1+1}{2\cdot {1}^{2}-11\cdot 1+5}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=1-4f(x)$ and $v=g(x).$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-4{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-(1-4f(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & =\frac{-4{f}^{′}(1)\cdot g(1)-(1-4f(1))\cdot {g}^{′}(1)}{(g(1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-4\cdot \frac{5}{8})\cdot \frac{2}{3}-(1-4\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}))\cdot (-1)}{{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{5}{3}+3)}{(\frac{4}{9})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{4}{9})} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-129626.problem:
At which value of $x\in (\frac{1}{2},5)$ does $f$ have a critical point?

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The function $f$ has a critical point at $x=$

                                        .
q-129626.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

In part 1, we obtained

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{-2({x}^{2}+2x-8)}{(2{x}^{2}-11x+5)^{2}}.
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-2({x}^{2}+2x-8)}{(2{x}^{2}-11x+5)^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-8 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+2x-8) & =0 \\ (x-2)(x+4) & =0 \\ x & =-4,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has two stationary points at $x=-4$ and $x=2.$ However, $x=-4$ does not lie in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},5),$ so we discard it.

- Second, we find the points in the domain of $f(x)$ where ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. Factoring our expression for ${f}^{′}(x),$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{-2(x-2)(x+4)}{[(2x-1)(x-5)]^{2}}.
$$

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist at $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=5.$ But these points do not lie in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},5).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the only critical point of $f(x)$ is $x=2.$

q-129628.problem:
Given that

$$
{\int }_{6}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=A{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x-1}+B{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-5}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants, find $A$ and $B.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $A=$

                                        {{field-2}}
q-129628.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator of $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)=\frac{x+1}{2{x}^{2}-11x+5}=\frac{x+1}{(2x-1)(x-5)}
$$

Our task is to find $A$ and $B$ such that

$$
\frac{x+1}{(2x-1)(x-5)}=\frac{A}{2x-1}+\frac{B}{x-5}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(2x-1)(x-5)$ gives

$$
x+1=A(x-5)+B(2x-1).
$$

Substituting $x=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5+1 & =A(5-5)+B(2\cdot 5-1) \\ 6 & =9B \\ B & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+1 & =A(\frac{1}{2}-5)+B(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\ \frac{3}{2} & =-\frac{9}{2}A \\ A & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{x+1}{(2x-1)(x-5)}=\frac{2}{3(x-5)}-\frac{1}{3(2x-1)}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{6}^{\infty }(\frac{2}{3(x-5)}-\frac{1}{3(2x-1)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-5}-\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A=-\frac{1}{3}$ and $B=\frac{2}{3}.$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{x+1}{2{x}^{2}-11x+5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-5}-\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's calculate the indefinite integral first. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{x-5}-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-5|-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{2{x}^{2}-11x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(|x-5|)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{(x-5)^{4}}{2x-1}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the improper integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{x+1}{2{x}^{2}-11x+5}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{(x-5)^{4}}{2x-1}|]}_{6}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{(a-5)^{4}}{2a-1}|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{11}|) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{(a-5)^{4}}{2a-1}|)-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{11}| \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$
